d: Monster hatched by a reptile from a cock’s egg; able to kill with a glance
ety: From Middle English cocatrice, from Old French cocatriz (“basilisk, cockatrice”), from Late Latin calcātrīx (“female trampler, treader”), from Latin calcāre (“to trample, to walk upon, to oppress”) + -trīx (“-ess: forming feminine agentives”), from calx (“heel”). Its eventual association with poultry influenced by cock (“rooster, male chicken”), q.v.
s: “Peace reigns in happy Luxor. The lion lies down with the lamb, and the child, if it will, may harmlessly put its hand into the cockatrice’s den.”

d: Call before a court to answer an indictment
ety: From Middle English areynen (“to interrogate, arraign, reprimand”), from Anglo-Norman areiner, arener, from Old French araisnier, areisnier, aresnier (“to speak to, address; accuse (in a law court)”) (whence modern French arraisonner (“to verify cargo, to arraign”)), from Vulgar Latin *arratiōnāre, from Latin adratiōnāre, from ad (“to”) + *ratiōnāre (“to reason, talk reasonably, talk”), from ratiō
s: He was arraigned in Washington, D.C., on the 25th of that month on charges of treason.

d: Affecting extreme elegance in dress and manner
ety: From fop + -ish.
s: They talked a delicate and elastic Arabic, and were mannered, often foppish, in habit.

d: Unpleasantly and excessively suave or ingratiating in manner or speech
ety: From Middle English fulsom, equivalent to full + -some. The meaning has evolved from an original positive connotation "abundant" to a neutral "plump" to a negative "overfed". In modern usage, it can take on any of these inflections. See usage note. The negative sense "offensive, gross; disgusting, sickening" developed secondarily after the 13th century and was influenced by Middle English foul (“f
s: Her fulsome timbre resonated throughout the hall.

d: An unrestrained expression of emotion
ety: From Old French ebullition, from Latin ēbullītiō, from ēbulliō (“to boil”).
s: His threats—his severe exclamations were but ebullitions of keen vexation, of agony of mind.

d: Someone who makes and sells hats
ety: The noun is a variant of Milaner (“(obsolete) inhabitant or native of Milan”) (referring to the importation and sale of women’s apparel, etc., made in Milan: see noun sense 1), from Late Middle English Milener, Miloner (“native of Milan”), from Milan + -er(e) (suffix denoting an inhabitant or resident). The verb is derived from the noun.
s: In the 1880s, milliners decorated hats with entire stuffed birds.

d: Occupied with or fond of the pleasures of good company
ety: Borrowed from French convivial, from Latin convīvium (“a feast”), combined form of con- (“together”) + vīvō (“to live”).
s: My grandpa was famously convivial.

d: Any long and tedious address or recital
ety: From Middle English, from Old French letanie, from Latin litania, from Ancient Greek λιτανεία (litaneía, “prayer”), from λιτή (litḗ, “prayer, entreaty”).
s: There are, to be sure, some differences in how the candidates propose addressing this litany of concerns.

d: Instructive (especially excessively)
ety: From French didactique, from Ancient Greek διδακτικός (didaktikós, “skilled in teaching”), from διδακτός (didaktós, “taught, learnt”), from διδάσκω (didáskō, “to teach, educate”). By surface analysis, didact + -ic.
s: The finest didactic poem in any language.

d: Being of equal extent or scope or duration
ety: From Latin conterminus, from con- (“with”) + terminus (“border, end”), equivalent to co- + terminous. The spelling with co- instead of con- is probably influenced by the related prefix co-.
s: New York's borough of Brooklyn and Kings County are coterminous.

d: Conceal one’s true motives from especially by elaborately feigning good intentions so as to gain an end
ety: Derivative of 17th-century vernacular bam (“to trick, to con”), which is a derivative of bam in noun use (fraudster, cheat). Possibly from French embobiner.
s: He's completely bamboozled by the changes in the computer system.

d: The courage to carry on
ety: From figurative use of metal (since 16th century). The two spellings were originally interchangeable variants, but came to be distinguished by sense in the 18th century.
s: By this Day and this Light, the fellow ha's mettell enough in his belly.

d: Lacking knowledge and understanding of mathematical concepts and methods
ety: From in- + numerate.
s: The worry is that we, as a society, will become innumerate, not just illiterate. A.I. appears to be exacerbating an alarming trend in which our basic education is failing our young citizens.

d: A sign of something about to happen
ety: Borrowed from Latin portentum, participle of portendere, from portendō (“to predict, to foretell”).
s: It was a portent of things to come.

d: Resembling or containing clay
ety: From Latin argillaceus, from argilla (“clay”), from Ancient Greek ἄργιλλος (árgillos, “white clay, potter's earth”), from ἀργός (argós, “white”).
s: The gleam of the land is in its rocks, the fine-grained argillaceous rocks, here, not purple or grey, but green of living stone.

d: Exhibiting an agreeably appropriate manner or style
ety: From felicity + -ous.
s: This sentence is grammatical; it is just not felicitous.

d: A traveler who drives (or travels with) a dog team
ety: From mush (“to drive dogs, usually pulling a sled, across snow”) + -er (suffix forming agent nouns). Mush is probably derived from French marche or marchons, respectively the second-person singular and first-person plural imperative forms of marcher (“to move; to travel; to walk”), from Proto-Germanic *markōną (“to mark; to notice”), from *marką (“mark; sign; stamp”), possibly related to *markō (“
s: A sled dog learns that by the time she's hungry, her musher has already prepared a meal; by the time she's tired, she has a warm bed.

d: The more conspicuous of two alternatives or cases or sides
ety: From Latin obversus, 1650s.
s: The medal had a cross on the obverse and had a name inscribed on the reverse.

d: Small two-wheeled horse-drawn carriage; with two seats and a folding hood
ety: Borrowed from French cabriolet.
s: "I think," said Isabella, startling Louisa, who had been watching the cabriolet down the street, "that Lady Penrhyn might have asked you to go with mamma."

d: A carving (or engraving) on whalebone, whale ivory, walrus tusk, etc., usually by American whalers
ety: The origin of the verb is unknown, but it has possibly been influenced by the surname Scrimshaw. Various etymologies have been proposed (for example, that it derives from scrimshank (“(Britain, military slang) to be idle, to shirk duty”)), but the Oxford English Dictionary does not consider any of them convincing. Following the surname theory, Etymonline ultimately derives the word probably from O
s: Rooney got his skull exposed, doggone it Soon he's gonna get scrimshaw carved on it

d: Carefree and happy and lighthearted
ety: From blithe + -some.
s: She made herself as blithesome as a lark, and at last she offered him two hundred dollars if he would sell her the whistle, and tell her how she should manage to get it safe home with her.

d: Having great beauty and splendor
ety: From Middle English splendiferous, from Medieval Latin splendiferus + -ous, from Late Latin splendōrifer, from Latin splendor + -fer (“bearing”). Reintroduced humorously into English c. 1837.
s: Hey boss, did you ever see a more splendiferous crash?

d: A kind of sideboard or buffet
ety: Borrowed from Italian credenza. Doublet of credence.
s: A recessed top story containing a cupboard was added to many credenze in the 16th cent. and this was usual in subsequent periods.

d: Strong feelings of embarrassment
ety: From French chagrin (“sorrow”), from Middle French chagrin (“pain, affliction”) (compare Middle French chagriner, chagrigner (“to experience sorrow”), Old French chagrin (“painful, afflicted”)), probably derived from Old Northern French chagreiner, chagraigner (“to sadden”), of uncertain origin. Likely an enlargement of Old French greignier, graignier (“to cringe, growl, be sullen, be angry, griev
s: To the chagrin of Rose, one of the younger women, Ginger, has never even learned to make perogi, Polish dumplings.

d: Being essentially equal to something
ety: First attested in English in 1628. Either inherited from an unattested Middle English borrowing from Anglo-Norman tant amount, from amunter, from tant (“as much”) amonter (“to amount to”) or borrowed in the early 17th century from Italian tanto montare (“to amount to as much”).
s: “Defendants’ representations to this Court that Mr. Musk is not running DOGE are tantamount to legal gaslighting,” CREW said.

d: A transverse and totally enclosed drain under a road or railway
ety: Origin obscure, with a number of possible etymologies suggested: * a dialectal word, * a word related to the name of the now-forgotten inventor, * a derivation from French couvert (“covered”), although couvert is not used in this sense and the French translation of culvert is ponceau or buse de drainage, * a derivation from an unrecorded Dutch word, possibly *coul-vaart, a combination of Dutch cou
s: A raft of twigs stayed upon a stone, suddenly detached itself, and floated towards the culvert.

d: Go against, as of rules and laws
ety: From Middle French contravenir (French contrevenir), from Latin contraveniō.
s: That the detention of the troops was a wise measure, is not to be contravened;

d: Of or occurring in summer
ety: From Middle English estival, from Old French estival, from Latin aestivalis.
s: The sky was a burnished aestival blue.

d: A loose outer coat usually of rich material
ety: From Middle English surcote, from Old French surcote, formed with sur (“over”) and cote (“coat, robe, tunic, overgarment”), respelled based on coat.
s: The Lord mayor and sheriff ride in their armour with surcoats of crimson.

d: An endowed church office giving income to its holder
ety: From Old French benefice, from Latin beneficium.
s: There were as many as one hundred thousand benefices offered during the period of his papacy, according to one chronicler and eyewitness.

d: Being sour to the taste
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin acidulus (“sourish, acidulous”), diminutive of acidus (“sour, acid”). See acid. By surface analysis, acid + -ule + -ous.
s: He talked with acidulous tolerance of the exalted personages who had sent Ashenden to X.

d: Being in agreement or harmony; often followed by ‘with’
ety: From Middle English acordaunt, equivalent to accord + -ant.
s: And now his voice accordant to the string.

d: Not to be placated or appeased or moved by entreaty
ety: From Middle French inexorable, from Latin inexōrābilis (“relentless, inexorable”) (or directly from the Latin word), from in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + exōrābilis (“that may be moved or persuaded by entreaty; exorable”). Exōrābilis is derived from exōrāre (from exōrō (“to persuade, win over; to beg, entreat, plead”), from ex- (prefix meaning ‘out of’) + ōrō (“to beg, entreat, plead, pray; to delive
s: No one, today, can miss the inexorable unfolding across the headlines and social media timelines of a transformed relationship between Britain and Europe.

d: A rectangular tiered temple or terraced mound erected by the ancient Assyrians and Babylonians
ety: Learned borrowing from Akkadian 𒅆𒂍𒉪 (ziqqurratum).
s: He works in an old ziggurat of an office building.

d: Remove completely from recognition or memory
ety: From Middle French effacer (“erase”), from Old French esfacier (“remove the face”).
s: Do not efface what I've written on the chalkboard.

d: A long (usually sleeveless) tunic of chain mail formerly worn as defensive armor
ety: From Middle English hauberk, from Old French hauberc, from Frankish *halsaberg (“neck-cover”).
s: The hauberk was to the Norman what the byrnie was to the Saxon, the chief method of bodily defence.

d: A temporary stay (e.g., as a guest)
ety: From Middle English sojourne (noun) and sojournen (verb), from Old French sojor, sojorner (modern séjour, séjourner), from (assumed) Vulgar Latin *subdiurnāre, from Latin sub- (“under, a little over”) + Late Latin diurnus (“lasting for a day”), from Latin dies (“day”).
s: Though long detain'd / In that obscure sojourn

d: Providing protective supervision; watching over or safeguarding
ety: From Latin tūtēlārius (“guardian”), from tūtēla (“tutelage, guardianship; dependent, client”) + -ārius (suffix denoting an agent of use); analysable as tutelar + -ary.
s: My uncle is always happy to discharge his tutelary responsibilities towards me.

d: A petty misdeed
ety: From Spanish pecadillo, diminutive form of pecado (“sin”), from Latin peccatum (“sin, error, fault”), from peccō (“to sin, offend”).
s: No sexual peccadillo is left unremarked upon.

d: Inclined to or marked by drowsiness
ety: First attested in 1615. Borrowed from French somnolent, from Old French sompnolent, from Latin somnolentus, from somnus (“sleep”).
s: As she reached toward the last few fiddleheads growing on the second hummock, her hand froze. She heard the somnolent buzzing of flies again.
